images.filename: THE CENTRAL BANK OF IRELAND (NEW HEADQUARTER BUILDING ON NORTH WALL QUAY)- ALONG BOTANIC AVENUE (JANUARY 2018)-135339 (27856990779).jpg
images.caption:
The Central Bank of Ireland  is Ireland's central bank, and as such part of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB). It is also the country's financial services regulator for most categories of financial firms. It was the issuer of Irish pound banknotes and coinage until the introduction of the euro currency, and now provides this service for the European Central Bank.
The Central Bank was founded on 1 February 1943 and since 1 January 1972 has been the banker of the Government of Ireland in accordance with the Central Bank Act 1971,which can be seen in legislative terms as completing the long transition from a currency board to a fully functional central bank.
Its head office was located on Dame Street, Dublin from 1979 until 2017. Its offices at Iveagh Court and College Green also closed down at the same time.

Since March 2017, its headquarters are located on North Wall Quay, where the public may exchange non-current Irish coinage and currency (both pre- and post-decimalization) for euros, as well as High Value Euro Currency Bank Notes and Mutilated Currency. It also operates from premises at nearby Spencer Dock. The Currency Centre at Sandyford is the currency manufacture, warehouse and distribution site of the bank.

images.filename: London and North Western Hotel, North Wall Quay, Dublin, Ireland.jpg
images.caption:
Appearing to the right in the picture of the MV Cill Airne floating restaurant on the river Liffey is the onetime Headquarters of the Black and Tans, officially the Royal Irish Constabulary Special Reserve. The building was attacked in the Irish War of Independence by the IRA in April 1921. 
Officially called the London and North Western Hotel, it was popularly known as the North Wall Quay hotel. The steamer service to and fro Holyhead in Wales departed from the North Wall Quay. 

In the photograph located behind the floating restaurant is the (closed) North Wall railway station or officially the London and North Western Railway station.

images.filename: Building number 1 Sir John Rogerson's Quay (1SJRQ).jpg
images.caption:
Number 1 Sir John Rogerson's Quay (or “1SJRQ” as the new office block is marketed as) was a tram depot when Dublin docks were booming. It served an important function, in transport in an light-industrial and commercial hub, and is a notable reminder of the maritime heritage of Dublin. The building dates to the 1820s when there was some re-development of the quay and a deepening of the channel along this part of the River Liffey. 
The 2010’s building has the historic tramway entrance, painstakingly restored. The tram depot extended from Rogerson's Quay along Creighton Street to the street Windmill Lane. Trams serviced the quay mainly transporting coal from ships berthed in the Liffey to the Gasworks on South Lotts Road in Ballsbridge.
